## Big Question {.role-slide}

How does a response distribution change with a linguistic predictor?

## Data {.role-slide}

More surprising words may take longer to read.

But words with the same surprisal still have different reading times.

## Challenge {.role-slide}

A regression must represent both the changing conditional mean and the remaining observation level variation.

## This Module {.role-slide .compact}

1. Define a straight line for one conditional mean.
2. Fit the line and quantify uncertainty.
3. Inspect residuals, leverage, and influence.
4. Add predictors, categorical contrasts, and interactions.
5. Address correlated predictors and changing conditional variance.

## One predictor {.section-slide}

From conditional means to a complete response model

## Question {.role-slide}

What is the expected log reading time among words with surprisal 4 bits?

## Answer {.role-slide}

A [conditional mean](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-reg.html) is the center of a response distribution at a specified predictor value:

$$m(x)=\mathbb E[Y\mid X=x].$$

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Regression Models: https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-reg.html
:::

## Answer {.role-slide}

A [regression model](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-reg.html) specifies how the conditional response distribution changes with predictors.

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Regression Models: https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-reg.html
:::

## Important Point #1 {.role-slide}

The marginal mean averages across the predictor distribution.

The conditional mean describes the response at one predictor value.

## Question {.role-slide}

What is the simplest restriction we can place on the conditional mean function?

## Answer {.role-slide}

[Simple linear regression](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=85) uses

$$m(x)=\beta_0+\beta_1x.$$

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

Winter, Statistics for Linguists, Chapter 6: https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=85
:::

## Interpretation {.role-slide}

$\beta_0$ is the expected response at $x=0$.

$\beta_1$ is the change in the expected response for a one unit increase in $x$.

## Question {.role-slide}

If $m(x)=5.70+.06x$, what are the expected log reading times at surprisal 2 and 7?

## Answer {.role-slide}

$$m(2)=5.82,\qquad m(7)=6.12.$$

The five bit increase corresponds to an expected increase of $.30$.

## Challenge {.role-slide}

The mean function alone assigns no probability to responses above or below the line.

## Answer {.role-slide}

Add normally distributed errors with constant variance:

$$Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\epsilon_i,\qquad \epsilon_i\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2).$$

## Important Point #2 {.role-slide}

A fitted association is not automatically causal.

The design and identifying assumptions determine whether a causal interpretation is available.

## Question {.role-slide}

What if zero is outside the observed predictor range?

## Answer {.role-slide}

[Centering](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=102) subtracts a declared reference value:

$$X_i^c=X_i-c.$$

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

Winter, Statistics for Linguists, Chapter 7: https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=102
:::

## Interpretation {.role-slide}

With $c=5$, the new intercept is the expected response at 5 bits.

The fitted predictions and distances among observations do not change.

## Important Point #3 {.role-slide}

Centering changes the origin. Scaling changes the unit.

The reference value must be reported.

## Question {.role-slide}

What if the response is positive and strongly right skewed?

## Possibility {.role-slide}

Model the logarithm of the response:

$$Z_i=\log Y_i.$$

## Interpretation {.role-slide}

An additive difference on the log scale corresponds to a multiplicative ratio on the original scale.

$$e^{\beta_1}$$

is the fitted ratio for a one unit predictor increase.

## Challenge {.role-slide}

The mean of $\log Y$ does not back transform mechanically into the mean of $Y$.

In general, $\mathbb E[Y]\neq e^{\mathbb E[\log Y]}$.

## Upshot {.role-slide}

The response scale, predictor reference, and mean function determine what every coefficient means.

## Fitting and uncertainty {.section-slide}

Choosing a line from observed responses

## Question {.role-slide}

Which candidate line lies closest to the observed responses?

## Answer {.role-slide}

[Least squares](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=85) minimizes

$$\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\widehat y_i)^2.$$

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

Winter, Statistics for Linguists, Chapter 6: https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=85
:::

## Method {.role-slide}

1. Choose candidate coefficients.
2. Compute each fitted conditional mean.
3. Subtract fitted from observed responses.
4. Square and add the discrepancies.

## Result #1 {.role-slide}

For one predictor,

$$\widehat\beta_1=\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)}{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2},\qquad \widehat\beta_0=\bar y-\widehat\beta_1\bar x.$$

## Important Point #1 {.role-slide}

With normally distributed errors and constant variance, least squares and [maximum likelihood](../../statistical-inference/maximum-likelihood.html) give the same coefficient estimates.

## Question {.role-slide}

How much would the fitted slope vary across repeated samples?

## Answer {.role-slide}

The slope standard error is the standard deviation of its [sampling distribution](../../statistical-inference/properties-of-estimators.html).

This recalls the [earlier definition of a standard error](../../statistical-inference/standard-errors.html).

## Interpretation {.role-slide}

In simple linear regression,

$$\operatorname{SE}(\widehat\beta_1)=\frac{\widehat\sigma}{\sqrt{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2}}.$$

## Important Point #2 {.role-slide}

Precision improves when residual variation is smaller or predictor values are more dispersed.

Precision does not establish model adequacy.

## Question {.role-slide}

How much squared error does the fitted line remove relative to a mean only model?

## Answer {.role-slide}

The [coefficient of determination](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=85) is

$$R^2=1-\frac{\mathrm{SSE}}{\mathrm{SST}}.$$

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

Winter, Statistics for Linguists, Chapter 6: https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=85
:::

## Answer {.role-slide}

The [total sum of squares](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=85) is $\mathrm{SST}=\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2$.

The [sum of squared errors](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=85) is $\mathrm{SSE}=\sum_i(y_i-\widehat y_i)^2$.

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

Winter, Statistics for Linguists, Chapter 6: https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=85
:::

## Important Point #3 {.role-slide}

Sample $R^2$ cannot decrease when predictors are added.

It is a within sample comparison, not an out of sample evaluation.

## Question {.role-slide}

How does Bayesian inference change the regression model?

## Answer {.role-slide}

[Bayesian linear regression](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-reg.html) adds [prior distributions](../../statistical-inference/posterior-distributions.html) for $\beta_0$, $\beta_1$, and $\sigma$.

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Regression Models: https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-reg.html
:::

## Method {.role-slide}

1. State priors in the units of each parameter.
2. Inspect [prior predictive responses](../../statistical-inference/prior-predictive-distributions.html).
3. Update with the likelihood.
4. Interpret [posterior distributions](../../statistical-inference/posterior-distributions.html) through contrasts on the response scale.

## Important Point #4 {.role-slide}

A prior that looks moderate on a coefficient scale may imply implausible responses.

Prior predictive checks reveal that implication before fitting.

## Upshot {.role-slide}

Fitting chooses coefficients. Inferential uncertainty concerns repeated samples or posterior distributions. Neither substitutes for checking the fitted model.

## Checking the fitted line {.section-slide}

Residuals, leverage, and influence

## Question {.role-slide}

What remains for one observation after subtracting its fitted conditional mean?

## Answer {.role-slide}

The [residual](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=85) is

$$e_i=y_i-\widehat y_i.$$

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

Winter, Statistics for Linguists, Chapter 6: https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=85
:::

## Important Point #1 {.role-slide}

A residual is observed after fitting.

An error term is an unobserved random variable in the model.

## Challenge {.role-slide}

Residuals may retain curvature, changing spread, asymmetric tails, or serial structure that the fitted model did not represent.

## Answer {.role-slide}

[Residual diagnostics](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=85) compare model predictions with observed residual patterns.

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

Winter, Statistics for Linguists, Chapter 6: https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=85
:::

## Method {.role-slide}

For each check, state the model prediction, identify the observable discrepancy, and explain its consequence for the linguistic analysis.

## Question {.role-slide}

Residual spread increases with articulation rate.

Which assumption fails: the linear mean or constant conditional variance?

## Answer {.role-slide}

Constant conditional variance fails.

The pattern alone does not establish that the conditional mean is nonlinear.

## Question {.role-slide}

Which observations occupy unusual positions among the predictor values?

## Answer {.role-slide}

[Leverage](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=85) measures unusual predictor position.

It does not use residual size.

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

Winter, Statistics for Linguists, Chapter 6: https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=85
:::

## Interpretation {.role-slide}

For simple linear regression,

$$h_{ii}=\frac{1}{n}+\frac{(x_i-\bar x)^2}{\sum_j(x_j-\bar x)^2}.$$

## Question {.role-slide}

How much would the fitted result change if one observation were omitted?

## Answer {.role-slide}

[Influence](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=85) measures dependence of a fitted result on a particular observation.

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

Winter, Statistics for Linguists, Chapter 6: https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=85
:::

## Important Point #2 {.role-slide}

High leverage is not automatically high influence.

Influence combines unusual predictor position with response discrepancy.

## Interpretation {.role-slide}

[Cook's distance](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=85) summarizes the fitted change under case deletion.

A large value motivates a sensitivity analysis, not automatic deletion.

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

Winter, Statistics for Linguists, Regression Diagnostics: https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=85
:::

## Upshot {.role-slide}

Residuals assess observation level discrepancies. Leverage concerns the design. Influence asks whether a result depends on a particular case.

## Several predictors {.section-slide}

Partial associations and matrix notation

## Question {.role-slide}

How does surprisal relate to reading time when word length is held fixed?

## Answer {.role-slide}

Extend the conditional mean:

$$m(x_1,x_2)=\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\beta_2x_2.$$

## Answer {.role-slide}

[Partial regression coefficients](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=119) describe one modeled association while the other predictors are held fixed.

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

Winter, Statistics for Linguists, Multiple Regression: https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=119
:::

## Important Point #1 {.role-slide}

Adding a predictor changes the interpretation of the coefficient.

A partial association can differ from the corresponding marginal association.

## Question {.role-slide}

How can one equation represent all observations and coefficients at once?

## Answer {.role-slide}

A [design matrix](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=133) places observations in rows and coefficient inputs in columns:

$$\boldsymbol\eta=\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta.$$

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

Winter, Statistics for Linguists, Categorical Predictors: https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=133
:::

## Interpretation {.role-slide}

One row of $\mathbf X$ describes one observation.

One column corresponds to one coefficient, not necessarily one original variable.

## Question {.role-slide}

How does a categorical predictor enter a numerical design matrix?

## Answer {.role-slide}

[Contrast coding](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=133) turns category levels into columns whose coefficients represent declared comparisons.

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

Winter, Statistics for Linguists, Categorical Predictors: https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=133
:::

## Approach {.role-slide}

Treatment coding makes the intercept the fitted mean for a reference category.

Each other coefficient compares one category with that reference.

## Important Point #2 {.role-slide}

Changing a full rank contrast coding changes coefficient meanings.

It does not change the fitted category means.

## Question {.role-slide}

What coding makes the intercept the unweighted average of fitted category means?

## Answer {.role-slide}

[Sum coding](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=133) uses contrast columns whose values sum to zero.

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

Winter, Statistics for Linguists, Categorical Predictors: https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=133
:::

## Important Point #3 {.role-slide}

The unweighted average of fitted category means is not necessarily the sample mean when category counts differ.

## Question {.role-slide}

How can ordered levels be compared through mutually orthogonal columns?

## Answer {.role-slide}

[Helmert coding](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=133) compares each level with a specified combination of later levels using orthogonal contrast columns.

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

Winter, Statistics for Linguists, Categorical Predictors: https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=133
:::

## Question {.role-slide}

What coding compares each later level with the average of earlier levels?

## Answer {.role-slide}

[Reverse Helmert contrasts](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/contrast.html) encode those earlier versus later comparisons.

The displayed matrix determines the sign and grouping.

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

R stats documentation, Contrast Matrices: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/contrast.html
:::

## Important Point #4 {.role-slide}

A contrast is meaningful only when its compared level groups answer a linguistic question.

Orthogonality alone does not supply that question.

## Upshot {.role-slide}

Several predictors change the estimand from a marginal to a partial association. The design matrix makes every coefficient comparison explicit.

## Interactions {.section-slide}

When one association depends on another predictor

## Challenge {.role-slide}

An additive model forces the surprisal slope to be identical across experimental conditions.

## Answer {.role-slide}

An [interaction term](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=149) allows one modeled association to depend on another predictor.

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

Winter, Statistics for Linguists, Interactions: https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=149
:::

## Method {.role-slide}

$$m(x,c)=\beta_0+\beta_1x+\beta_2c+\beta_3xc.$$

The coefficient $\beta_3$ is a difference between slopes.

## Question {.role-slide}

What is the surprisal slope when $c=0$? What is it when $c=1$?

## Answer {.role-slide}

$$\text{slope at }c=0:\ \beta_1$$

$$\text{slope at }c=1:\ \beta_1+\beta_3$$

## Important Point #1 {.role-slide}

Keep the lower order terms when adding the product term.

Their meanings become conditional on the other predictor being zero.

## Important Point #2 {.role-slide}

An interaction is a property of the modeled conditional mean on a declared scale.

It does not by itself identify a causal mechanism.

## Upshot {.role-slide}

Interpret an interaction through fitted comparisons at meaningful predictor values, not through the product coefficient in isolation.

## Correlated predictors {.section-slide}

What the data can distinguish

## Challenge {.role-slide}

Two predictors may vary together so strongly that many coefficient pairs produce almost the same fitted values.

## Answer {.role-slide}

[Collinearity](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=119) is linear overlap among predictors.

Perfect collinearity makes separate coefficients unidentified.

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

Winter, Statistics for Linguists, Multiple Regression: https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=119
:::

## Important Point #1 {.role-slide}

Strong collinearity can make separate coefficients unstable while fitted predictions remain stable in the observed predictor region.

## Question {.role-slide}

How much does predictor overlap increase a coefficient's sampling variance?

## Answer {.role-slide}

The [variance inflation factor](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=119) for predictor $j$ is

$$\operatorname{VIF}_j=\frac{1}{1-R_j^2}.$$

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

Winter, Statistics for Linguists, Multiple Regression: https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=119
:::

## Important Point #2 {.role-slide}

A VIF has no universal cutoff that answers the linguistic question.

Inspect which predictor contrasts the observed design actually supports.

## Question {.role-slide}

Can estimation prefer smaller coefficients when correlated predictors permit many similar fits?

## Answer {.role-slide}

The [residual sum of squares](https://www.statlearning.com/s/ISLRSeventhPrinting.pdf) is

$$\mathrm{RSS}=\sum_i(y_i-\widehat y_i)^2.$$

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

James et al., An Introduction to Statistical Learning: https://www.statlearning.com/s/ISLRSeventhPrinting.pdf
:::

## Answer {.role-slide}

[Ridge regression](https://islp.readthedocs.io/en/latest/labs/Ch06-varselect-lab.html#ridge-regression-and-the-lasso) minimizes

$$\mathrm{RSS}+\lambda\sum_{j=1}^p\beta_j^2.$$

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

ISLP Laboratory, Ridge Regression and the Lasso: https://islp.readthedocs.io/en/latest/labs/Ch06-varselect-lab.html#ridge-regression-and-the-lasso
:::

## Answer {.role-slide}

The [regularization parameter](https://islp.readthedocs.io/en/latest/labs/Ch06-varselect-lab.html#ridge-regression-and-the-lasso) $\lambda$ controls the strength of shrinkage.

Predictors should be put on comparable scales before applying the penalty.

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

ISLP Laboratory, Ridge Regression and the Lasso: https://islp.readthedocs.io/en/latest/labs/Ch06-varselect-lab.html#ridge-regression-and-the-lasso
:::

## Important Point #3 {.role-slide}

Ridge regression stabilizes estimation under overlap.

It does not recover uniquely meaningful effects for perfectly redundant predictors.

## Question {.role-slide}

What remains of one predictor after its linear association with the others is removed?

## Answer {.role-slide}

[Residualization](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jml.2013.12.003) replaces a predictor by residuals from a regression on the remaining predictors.

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

Wurm and Fisicaro, What residualizing predictors in regression analyses does: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jml.2013.12.003
:::

## Important Point #4 {.role-slide}

A residualized predictor is not a purified linguistic construct.

It is a sample dependent linear discrepancy from a specified auxiliary regression.

## Upshot {.role-slide}

Correlated predictors limit attribution. VIF describes the uncertainty increase, ridge changes estimation, and residualization changes the predictor representation.

## Changing conditional variance {.section-slide}

Modeling scale as well as location

## Question {.role-slide}

What is the standard term for residual spread that changes across predictor values?

## Answer {.role-slide}

[Heteroscedasticity](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=85) is nonconstant conditional variance.

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

Winter, Statistics for Linguists, Chapter 6: https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=85
:::

## Important Point #1 {.role-slide}

A changing mean and changing variance are different patterns.

Residual spread should be inspected around the fitted conditional mean.

## Challenge {.role-slide}

Ordinary linear regression uses one $\sigma$ for every predictor value.

That restriction can distort uncertainty when the response spread changes systematically.

## Question {.role-slide}

How can a predictor change the scale parameter of the response distribution?

## Answer {.role-slide}

[Distributional regression](https://paulbuerkner.com/brms/articles/brms_distreg.html) assigns separate predictor equations to different distributional parameters.

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

Bürkner, Distributional Models in brms: https://paulbuerkner.com/brms/articles/brms_distreg.html
:::

## Method {.role-slide}

$$\mu_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i$$

$$\log\sigma_i=\gamma_0+\gamma_1x_i$$

The logarithm keeps $\sigma_i$ positive.

## Interpretation {.role-slide}

$\beta_1$ describes change in the conditional mean.

$e^{\gamma_1}$ describes the multiplicative change in conditional standard deviation.

## Important Point #2 {.role-slide}

Add a predictor equation only for a distributional parameter that the design and theory require.

Flexibility alone is not a reason to model every parameter.

## Interim Discussion {.role-slide}

Linear regression begins with a conditional mean. Each extension changes one part of the model while preserving the meaning of the earlier parts.

## Conclusion {.section-slide}

What the linear model now permits

## Big Question {.role-slide}

How does a response distribution change with a linguistic predictor?

## Answer {.role-slide .compact}

1. A linear regression describes conditional response distributions.
2. Coefficients require a declared response scale and predictor reference.
3. Fitting, uncertainty, and model checking answer different questions.
4. Multiple predictors define partial associations through a design matrix.
5. Interactions, regularization, and distributional regression each relax one distinct restriction.

## Question {.role-slide}

For the fitted linguistic claim, which response feature changes, with respect to which predictor contrast, and under which model assumptions?
